title: DockPilot finds late trucks a slot they can really use, holds it safely, and hands the rest to a person
lede: A progress note in plain words. DockPilot helps a warehouse when trucks run late: it works out which unloading slots still fit, offers the best ones, and makes sure two drivers can never be given the same slot. Built on the practice data from 4 August 2026.

journey.title: Can this slot work?
journey.text: Checks a slot against 15 rules: weight, dock type, arrival time, unload time, opening hours, breakdowns, and more.

journey.title: Find the best options
journey.text: Looks at every slot for the rest of the day and picks the top 3 that pass every rule.

journey.title: Hold it for 10 minutes
journey.text: Reserves the chosen slot while the driver confirms. Nobody else can take it. Unused holds free themselves.

journey.title: Warehouse confirms
journey.text: The driver says yes and the hold becomes a booking request. The warehouse confirms or rejects it; no answer in 30 minutes goes to a coordinator.

journey.title: Hand to a person
journey.text: When nothing fits, a coordinator gets the full story at once: who, the current booking, the real arrival time, every slot tried and why it failed.

example.title: A real example from the data: truck SHP1014

timeline.text: The driver of a critical load (21 tonnes, 75 minutes to unload) says they'll arrive at 11:25.
The old system had booked them into the 11:00 slot on dock D1. DockPilot shows that slot fails three ways: **arrives too late**, **too heavy for the dock** and **unload too long for the slot**.
DockPilot offers dock D2 12:00–14:00, dock D4 12:00–14:00, or dock D2 13:00–15:00. It uses two slots in a row, because 75 minutes doesn't fit in one hour.
The driver picks D2. It's held until 09:55. Another driver who asks for the same slot is told it's taken.
Nobody confirmed, so the hold ran out by itself and the slot is free for others again.

why: The client's current system accepted that 11:00 booking without complaint. DockPilot refuses it, and says why in plain words.
A slot can't sit locked all day because someone forgot to answer.
If a chat app sends the same message twice, the driver still gets one hold, not two.
Every hold placed, released or expired is written to a log, so we can always explain what happened and when.

blocks.name: Project set-up
blocks.what: Creates the project and stores the client's data package exactly as received, with fingerprints that prove it never changes.

blocks.name: Working copy
blocks.what: Makes a copy of the client's database to work on, and adds three new tables: holds, hand-offs to people, and a log of everything that happens. The original is only ever read.

blocks.name: Clock and settings
blocks.what: A clock that tests can wind forward, so "10 minutes later" takes a split second to test. All agreed numbers (hold times, buffers, timeouts) live in one settings file.

blocks.name: Slot check
blocks.what: Answers "can this truck use this slot?" and lists every reason if not: wrong dock, too heavy, too late, unload too long, dock broken, slot taken, and so on.

blocks.name: Find options
blocks.what: Builds every sensible choice (one slot, or two back-to-back for long unloads), checks each, and ranks the passing ones: earliest first.

blocks.name: Safe hold
blocks.what: Reserves the chosen slot for 10 minutes (5 when it's very busy). One request at a time, so two drivers can never both win the same slot.

blocks.name: Hand-off to a person
blocks.what: When no slot fits, writes the full story for a coordinator: who, what, latest arrival time, every option tried and why it failed.

blocks.name: Warehouse confirmation
blocks.what: Turns a hold into a booking request the warehouse confirms or rejects, and chases if they don't answer in time.

blocks.name: Changes during the day
blocks.what: Handles new arrival times, reschedules, no-shows and dock breakdowns that hit bookings already made.

blocks.name: Message reader
blocks.what: Reads a driver's message and picks out what they want and when they'll arrive, using simple rules.

blocks.name: AI message reader
blocks.what: Uses an AI model to read messages more flexibly, falling back to the simple rules if it's unavailable.

blocks.name: Driver login
blocks.what: Only a real driver with a trip in progress or a booked slot can chat: phone number plus a one-time code.

blocks.name: Conversation
blocks.what: Talks with the driver: asks one clear question when needed, offers options, and always explains a refusal.

blocks.name: Web chat page
blocks.what: A simple local web page: the driver logs in, then chats with DockPilot like on WhatsApp; a warehouse view confirms or rejects requests.

blocks.name: Driver never left waiting
blocks.what: The driver always hears something: right after picking a slot, while the warehouse decides, and when the warehouse is too slow and a coordinator takes over. Found in a live test.

blocks.name: Fair choice between trucks
blocks.what: Decides who gets a slot when several trucks want it, with priority loads protected and close calls sent to a person.

blocks.name: Stress test
blocks.what: Many programs race for one slot, 100 times over, to prove nothing is ever double-booked.

blocks.name: Replay of real cases
blocks.what: Replays the client's recorded cases end to end and reports the results.

blocks.name: Write-up
blocks.what: Explains DockPilot and how to run it, with examples from the replays.

blocks.name: See every step (trace mode)
blocks.what: A switch that records every step a message goes through, including exactly what the AI was asked and answered, or why it wasn't used. Shown in the chat, the terminal and LangSmith.

blocks.name: Ready for bad data
blocks.what: If a driver's booking record can't be true (too heavy for the dock, two trucks on one slot), DockPilot says so with the reason, offers to find a slot that fits, and tells a coordinator. It never edits the client's data.

blocks.name: Changes during the day, live
blocks.what: The web demo now notices a broken dock, a missed slot or a new arrival time when it happens, re-homes or offers new slots, and tells the driver if they're chatting.

choices.title: Timings
items: Hold a slot for 10 minutes, or 5 when 5+ requests arrive within 10 minutes.
Wait 30 minutes for the warehouse to confirm before a coordinator chases.
Add 30 minutes of slack when a driver's arrival estimate is vague.

choices.title: Rules
items: Show the driver at most 3 options at a time.
One hold per truck: picking a new slot releases the old one.
Any dock problem (breakdown, maintenance, slowdown) blocks the slot.
A slot starting at exactly 21:00 is allowed; later starts need approval.
Weight limits are checked against the load only, for now.

limits: Honest limits today: the login code is shown on screen instead of sent by SMS, and the chat is a local web page (no WhatsApp yet). Coordinators see hand-offs but can't mark them handled or move another truck's booking yet. A driver's own limits ("after 12", "must leave by 1:30") are read but not yet used to choose slots, and a no-show truck isn't messaged. Timings the client hasn't confirmed run on stated defaults.
